title: The Conversion Deadlock (Read-Then-Update the Same Row)
description: Two sessions that read then update the same row under REPEATABLE READ deadlock upgrading shared locks to exclusive; an UPDLOCK hint on the read serializes them. Why it matters: this deadlock shape is subtler than the classic textbook case and catches experienced developers off guard, since it can occur on a single row with no obvious lock-order mistake.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About

Imagine two people each holding a "reserved" sign on the same seat, each intending to eventually sit down in it, each politely waiting for the other's sign to be removed first before they'll remove their own. Neither one is doing anything wrong individually — reserving a seat before sitting is reasonable — but if both insist on waiting for the other's reservation to clear first, neither will ever move. This lesson is about a specific, well-known deadlock shape in SQL Server that happens not because two transactions touch things in opposite order (as in the earlier deadlock lesson) but because two transactions do the *exact same* read-then-update sequence on the *exact same* row, at the same time.

**What this lesson's topic actually is.** This lesson is about the "conversion deadlock," so named because it involves upgrading, or "converting," a shared lock into an exclusive lock — and about what happens when two sessions both try to perform that same upgrade on the same row simultaneously, under an isolation level called REPEATABLE READ.

**Why this happens in real databases.** A common and completely reasonable pattern is "read a row first to check its current value, then update it based on what you saw" — for instance, reading an account balance, checking there's enough money, then debiting it. Under REPEATABLE READ isolation, a level stronger than the ordinary default, SQL Server guarantees that once you've read a row within a transaction, nobody else can change it before your transaction finishes — a genuinely useful guarantee for exactly this "check then update" pattern. But delivering that guarantee requires holding a lock on the row from the moment you read it, and that requirement is exactly what sets up this particular deadlock shape when two sessions do it to the same row at once.

**How it happens mechanically inside SQL Server.** Under REPEATABLE READ, a plain `SELECT` still takes a shared lock on the rows it reads — same as under ordinary READ COMMITTED — but crucially, it *holds* that shared lock until the transaction ends, rather than releasing it right after the read, specifically to guarantee nobody else can change the row before you do. Now imagine two sessions, A and B, both start a transaction and both run the exact same `SELECT ... WHERE AccountId = 1` against the same row, at nearly the same instant. Shared locks are compatible with other shared locks, so both A and B successfully acquire a shared lock on that row simultaneously — no conflict yet. Then both sessions proceed to their next statement: an `UPDATE` on that same row, based on what they just read. An `UPDATE` needs an exclusive lock, but each session already holds a shared lock of its own on that row — to proceed, each session needs to "convert" its own shared lock into an exclusive lock. That conversion requires that no *other* session still holds a shared lock on the same row at the same time. But A is holding a shared lock that B needs cleared before B can convert, and B is holding a shared lock that A needs cleared before A can convert — each session is waiting for the other's shared lock to release, and neither will release its own shared lock until its own conversion succeeds. That's a deadlock, structurally identical in spirit to the opposite-order deadlock covered elsewhere, but arising from lock *upgrading* on the *same* row instead of lock *ordering* across *different* rows.

**Why this matters in production.** This deadlock shape is extremely common in exactly the kind of "read the current value, then update based on it" logic that shows up constantly in real business transactions — balance checks before debits, stock checks before decrementing inventory, status checks before transitioning a workflow — anywhere code deliberately reads a row first specifically to make a decision about how to update it, under an isolation level strong enough to guarantee the row won't change out from under it in between. Because it requires two sessions to race on the exact same row at nearly the same instant, it's intermittent and hard to reproduce deliberately, showing up as a periodic, confusing deadlock error under real concurrent load on hot rows, even though the code "just reads, then updates" in what looks like an obviously safe sequence.

The fix demonstrated in this lesson is to add an `UPDLOCK` hint to the initial `SELECT` — this tells SQL Server to take an update lock (a special lock type designed exactly for this "I'm about to update what I'm reading" situation) instead of an ordinary shared lock, right from the read. Unlike shared locks, only one session can hold an update lock on a given row at a time, so if two sessions try to read-with-`UPDLOCK` the same row simultaneously, the second one simply waits its turn cleanly for the first one's entire transaction to complete, rather than both proceeding into the read step in parallel and colliding later during the upgrade. Serializing the very first read this way eliminates the race entirely, converting what would have been a deadlock into a normal, safe wait.

**Try it yourself.** The scenario below has both sessions read the same row under REPEATABLE READ and then try to update it, and shows you the resulting deadlock as each session's lock conversion collides with the other's held shared lock. After adding `UPDLOCK` to the initial read in both sessions, re-run the same interleaving and watch the deadlock disappear — the second session now simply waits cleanly for the first session's whole transaction to finish, rather than both proceeding into a doomed simultaneous upgrade.

**Beyond this exact scenario.** This deadlock shape is specific to isolation levels that hold read locks for the duration of the transaction — REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE — and does not occur under the ordinary READ COMMITTED default, because a plain read under READ COMMITTED releases its shared lock immediately rather than holding it until commit, leaving nothing to collide with during a later update. This is one more reason isolation level should be a deliberate choice tied to what a transaction genuinely needs, rather than a default reached for without considering the locking behavior it actually implies.

## Scenario
Two money-transfer sessions run the same classic pattern against Alice's account inside a **`REPEATABLE READ`** transaction (chosen so the balance they read stays stable): **read the current balance, then update it**. Individually they're fine. Run them at the same time and one is killed as a **deadlock victim** — even though they only ever touch a *single* row.

## Why it deadlocks
This is a **conversion deadlock**, and it needs no opposing lock order. Both sessions `SELECT` account 1 first, each taking a **shared (S)** lock — and S locks are compatible, so both succeed. Under `REPEATABLE READ` that S lock is **held to the end of the transaction** (unlike the default `READ COMMITTED`, which drops it the instant the read finishes). Then each session's `UPDATE` tries to convert its still-held S lock to an **exclusive (X)** lock — incompatible with the *other* session's S lock — so each waits for the other to let go. Neither can, and the deadlock monitor kills one.

## What to look for
- Both sessions **acquire** an S lock on `Accounts(1)`, then both try to **convert to X** and block on each other.
- The deadlock graph shows a lock-conversion cycle on the same resource (not two different rows).

## The concept
Reordering rows can't help — there's only one row. The fix is to declare *update intent at read time* so the two reads can't both succeed. Add an **`UPDLOCK`** hint to the `SELECT`: `SELECT ... FROM Accounts WITH (UPDLOCK) WHERE AccountId = 1`. `UPDLOCK` takes an **update (U)** lock, which is incompatible with another U — so the second session simply *waits* at the read instead of racing to a doomed conversion. One transaction completes, then the other proceeds. (`sp_getapplock` or serializing the work are heavier alternatives.)
startingQuery: -- This is a concurrency lesson. Add WITH (UPDLOCK) to each session's SELECT and Run the interleaving.
hints: Both sessions take a shared (S) lock on the same row during the SELECT, then both try to upgrade to exclusive (X). That mutual upgrade is the deadlock.
There is only one row, so reordering access can't help. You need to stop both reads from co-existing.
Add WITH (UPDLOCK) to each SELECT so the read takes an update (U) lock; the second session then waits instead of deadlocking: SELECT Balance FROM Accounts WITH (UPDLOCK) WHERE AccountId = 1;

interleaving.description: Both sessions read Alice's balance (shared lock), then update it (exclusive lock) — the mutual S-to-X conversion deadlocks.

A.sql: SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ; BEGIN TRAN; SELECT Balance FROM Accounts WHERE AccountId = 1;
UPDATE Accounts SET Balance = Balance - 100 WHERE AccountId = 1; COMMIT;

B.sql: SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ; BEGIN TRAN; SELECT Balance FROM Accounts WHERE AccountId = 1;
UPDATE Accounts SET Balance = Balance - 50 WHERE AccountId = 1; COMMIT;

interleaving.solutionNote: Add WITH (UPDLOCK) to each session's SELECT so the read takes an update (U) lock. U locks are mutually exclusive, so the second session blocks at the read and waits instead of both racing to convert S->X; one transaction commits, then the other completes.
